title: The Concubine Who Invented Korean Movable Metal Type
event_summary: During the Mongol invasions of Korea, the Goryeo court fled to Ganghwa Island and there commissioned the casting of the world's first verified metal movable type to reprint the entire Buddhist canon, the Tripitaka. The official Choe Yun-ui oversaw the project, which produced the 'Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun' — a massive compilation of ritual texts printed using individually cast bronze type characters, predating Gutenberg by over 200 years. The enterprise was driven by a desperate belief that printing sacred Buddhist texts would invoke divine protection against the Mongol onslaught.
why_forgotten: The original printed books from 1234 were destroyed during continued Mongol raids, leaving only textual references in later Korean records rather than surviving physical copies. European historiography long credited Gutenberg as the inventor of movable type printing, and Cold War-era division of Korea further complicated international scholarly attention. The achievement was also overshadowed by the later Jikji of 1377, the oldest surviving metal-type printed book, which itself remained obscure until a French collector's copy surfaced in the 20th century.
why_it_matters: This event demonstrates that the most transformative technology in human communication — mechanical reproduction of text — originated in East Asia, not Europe, fundamentally challenging Western-centric narratives of innovation. The Korean technique of casting individual metal characters influenced subsequent printing developments across East Asia and raises profound questions about how technology diffuses globally. Today, UNESCO recognizes the Jikji as a Memory of the World, and the 1234 precedent has reshaped how historians understand the origins of the information revolution that ultimately led to mass literacy, the Reformation, and the modern press.
